questions.q: How does a webhook differ from the REST API calls covered earlier in this chapter?
options: A webhook always uses GET instead of POST
A webhook is an inbound request the provider sends to you when an event happens, instead of your script asking for data
A webhook requires no authentication at all, ever
A webhook is just a renamed term for a regular API call
questions.explain: A webhook reverses the usual direction: instead of your script polling an API for changes, the provider pushes an HTTP POST to your server the moment an event occurs.

questions.q: Why must Northbridge's webhook receiver verify a signature before trusting the payload?
options: Signature verification is only needed for GET requests
Because the receiving URL must be reachable from the internet, anyone could POST a fake event to it without a way to prove the request's origin
Flask requires a signature header or it won't start the server
Verification makes the server respond faster
questions.explain: A webhook URL is necessarily public so the provider can reach it, which means anyone could send a forged request; verifying the HMAC signature is the only way to confirm it genuinely came from the carrier.

questions.q: Why is the HMAC computed over request.data (the raw request bytes) rather than the parsed JSON object?
options: Raw bytes are required because Flask cannot parse JSON
Re-serializing parsed JSON can produce different bytes than what the carrier actually signed, breaking the comparison
It makes the hash shorter
hashlib only works on raw bytes, never on dictionaries, by any method
questions.explain: The carrier signs the exact bytes it sent. Parsing that JSON and re-serializing it can change whitespace or key order, producing different bytes and a mismatched hash even for a legitimate request.

questions.q: Why does the example use hmac.compare_digest(signature, expected) instead of signature == expected?
options: compare_digest() is simply a faster string comparison with no security benefit
A plain == comparison exits early on a mismatch, leaking timing information an attacker could use to guess the correct signature a byte at a time; compare_digest() runs in constant time
== cannot compare two strings in Python
compare_digest() automatically decodes the request body
questions.explain: compare_digest() performs a constant-time comparison specifically to prevent timing attacks, where an attacker measures how long a comparison takes to narrow down the correct signature character by character.

questions.q: In the handler, what should happen before handle_shipment_event(event) is ever called?
options: Nothing — it's safe to call it as soon as request.get_json() returns
The signature must be verified with compare_digest() and confirmed valid first
The server should be restarted
The event type must be printed to the console
questions.explain: Acting on the event's contents should only happen after the signature check has confirmed the request genuinely came from the carrier — verify first, then parse and act.
